# Acceleration and Sparse Structures

Also called: Spatial Partitioning, Visual Hull Culling, Block-based NeRF

## Overview
This family of methods accelerates [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) training and rendering by reducing the volume of space queried by the neural network, addressing the computational bottleneck of sampling empty space or redundant regions in large scenes. Unlike [Zip-NeRF Training Procedure](9538-zip-nerf-training-procedure.md) which uses caching to reduce gradient variance, or [Adaptive Ray Sampling](8870-adaptive-ray-sampling.md) which varies density along rays, these methods explicitly restrict the spatial domain of queries using geometric hulls, spatial partitioning, or block [decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md).

## Shared principles
The core mechanism is spatial culling or decomposition. Instead of sampling points uniformly or density-based across the entire scene bounding box, these methods maintain a data structure ([voxel grid, block](#13837-voxel-chunk-management.md) list, or cache) that identifies "empty" or "irrelevant" regions. Queries to the neural network are either skipped entirely or restricted to a subset of the scene. This reduces the number of forward passes through the MLP, directly lowering training and inference time.

## Subtopics

### [Zip-NeRF Training Procedure](9538-zip-nerf-training-procedure.md)
Uses a hybrid radiance cache ([Fast Cache](#9552-fast-cache-control-variate-radiance-cache.md) and NeRF-cache) as a control variate to correct bias in [gradient estimation](#6476-gradient-estimation-our-grad.md), allowing for efficient joint optimization of materials and environment maps.

### [VaxNeRF](11379-vaxnerf.md)
Restricts ray sampling to the visual hull $V$, defined by the intersection of camera frustums and foreground masks, eliminating queries to empty space outside the object silhouette.

### [Block-NeRF](13537-block-nerf.md)
Scales to city-scale scenes by partitioning the environment into overlapping spatial blocks, training independent NeRFs per block, and using a visibility MLP to composite results, handling transient objects via semantic masking.

### Spatial Partitioning
A strategy to create tiles that ensures balanced workload across GPUs by recursively partitioning space based on a sparse point cloud or sampled rays, ensuring each tile contains a comparable number of points.

### Spatial Partitioning
- **Definition**: A strategy to create tiles that ensures balanced workload (similar number of network evaluations/ray samples) across GPUs, avoiding suboptimal GPU utilization caused by uneven scene content distribution [S1].
- **Step**: If a sparse point cloud is available, recursively identify the plane where the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) equals 0.5 for the 3D point distribution along each axis to partition space [S1]. If no sparse point cloud is available, discretize randomly sampled training rays into 3D samples to estimate scene content distribution, then partition similarly [S1].
- **Parameter**: Partitioning runs typically within seconds [S1].

## Background
The original NeRF [G] samples points uniformly or by density along rays, which is inefficient for scenes with large empty spaces or complex geometry. [VaxNeRF](#11379-vaxnerf.md) [S1] introduced visual hull culling to remove empty space queries. [Block-NeRF](#13537-block-nerf.md) [S1] addressed the scalability of NeRF to city-scale data by decomposing the scene. NeRF-XL [S1] introduced spatial partitioning to balance multi-GPU workloads.
